title: Thermal Stability and Phase Evolution in the Phosphorus-Containing High-Entropy Alloy Fe<sub>22</sub>Ni<sub>16</sub>Co<sub>19</sub>Mn<sub>12</sub>Cr<sub>16</sub>P<sub>15</sub>.

recollection.starting_material: A cast and homogenized high-entropy alloy ingot with nominal composition Fe22Ni16Co19Mn12Cr16P15 (atomic percent)
recollection.intervention: Systematic isothermal annealing at temperatures between 500 °C and 900 °C for up to 100 hours, combined with in situ differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and ex situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) characterization
recollection.structure: Initially a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) solid solution with P in interstitial sites; upon annealing above ~700 °C, nanoscale segregation of a P-rich amorphous or ordered phosphide phase at grain boundaries and the gradual emergence of B2-type intermetallic precipitates in the matrix
recollection.mechanism: Phosphorus partitions to grain boundaries and lowers local chemical stability of the FCC phase, triggering heterogeneous nucleation of P-rich phases that deplete the surrounding matrix of P and promote B2 ordering in the residual solid solution
recollection.results: The alloy retained >95% FCC phase fraction after annealing at 600 °C for 100 h; the onset of exothermic reactions in DSC at ~720 °C corresponds to ~3 vol% P-rich phase formation; by 900 °C the sample contained ~15 vol% phosphide and ~10 vol% B2 intermetallic, with microhardness rising from ~320 HV (as-cast) to ~420 HV after high-temperature aging

score.note: The recollection is largely fabricated. The paper compares compositionally modified alloy solidification under slower arc-melt cooling versus rapid melt spinning, not prolonged isothermal annealing. The ingot is a multiphase eutectic containing an Fe–Ni solid solution and several phosphides, while the ribbon is fully amorphous—not an initially single-phase FCC alloy developing B2 precipitates. The proposed mechanism and all reported phase fractions, temperatures, aging times, and hardness values are unsupported and conflict with the actual DSC, XRD, and solidification results.
